facts.label: Written brief before casting starts
Hook options in every script
Beats in every shot list
Pages, so you actually read it

features.title: One thing the ad has to say.
features.body: Before the hook, before the creator, one sentence: the pain point, the payoff or the offer this ad exists to land. Every brief opens with it, and everything below it is checked against it. An ad that tries to say five things says none of them.

bullets.title: A single sentence, not a list
bullets.body: We write the core message as one line you can read back to yourself. If it needs a comma and an 'also', it is two ads.

bullets.title: Must-say claims, separated
bullets.body: Pricing, ingredients, results and anything with legal weight are listed word for word, apart from the lines a creator can say their own way.

bullets.title: Checked against the offer
bullets.body: The message is matched to what the landing page actually says before the brief leaves us, so the ad and the page agree.

features.visual: White card 400×300. Header 'THE ONE THING' in uppercase 12px grey. Below, a single sentence in 16px black on a soft sand highlight. Beneath it two column blocks: 'MUST SAY' with two lines each ending in a small tick, and 'IN YOUR OWN WORDS' with two lighter grey lines. Footer chip 'Matches the landing page'.

features.title: The hook, written out, not described.
features.body: 'Start with something attention-grabbing' is a wish, not a hook. Every brief carries the first line, actually written, with alternatives the creator can choose between or riff on. The opening seconds are the only part of the ad we never leave to improvisation.

bullets.title: Eight lines to choose from
bullets.body: Each script ships with eight opening lines across different patterns, so the shoot has real options rather than one bet.

bullets.title: Shortlisted with you
bullets.body: You mark the ones you would run before anyone films. The creator gets the shortlist, not the whole list.

bullets.title: Paired with the platform
bullets.body: A pattern-interrupt line for the For You page, a quieter first-person line for Reels. The brief says which is for where.

features.visual: White card 400×330 titled 'HOOKS · 8'. Eight rows of 14px text, each with a small number 01–08 left; rows 03 and 06 carry a jam tick and a 'shoot' chip; the others are grey. Footer: 'Shortlist agreed with your brand'.

features.title: A shot list, not a script for every word.
features.body: Scripting every syllable produces stiff, obviously scripted content, which defeats the point of UGC. Instead the brief gives the creator five beats to hit and lets them fill in the phrasing around the required claims.

bullets.title: Five beats, every time
bullets.body: Problem, discovery, demo, payoff, call to action. Each beat is a line or two of intent, not dialogue.

bullets.title: Room for the creator's voice
bullets.body: Anything not marked must-say is theirs to phrase. That is what keeps it sounding like a person and not a read.

bullets.title: Length and ratio set per placement
bullets.body: Vertical 9:16, the target length and the pacing note are written in for each platform the ad is going to.

features.visual: White card 400×320 titled 'SHOT LIST'. A vertical list of five beats, each a numbered row (01 Problem, 02 Discovery, 03 Demo, 04 Payoff, 05 Call to action) with a one-line grey description and a small duration tag on the right ('0–3s', '3–8s', …). A thin vertical rule connects the numbers.

features.title: Tone shown, not adjectived.
features.body: 'Fun, authentic, punchy' gets read five ways by five creators. Every brief links one or two reference videos so tone is a thing you can watch, and lists the do's and don'ts that most often cause a reshoot.

bullets.title: Two references, linked
bullets.body: Yours or a competitor's. A creator watches them once and knows what 'natural' means for your brand.

bullets.title: Do's and don'ts next to the shot list
bullets.body: No visible competitor logos, no unapproved claims, no music with lyrics, no slow zoom on the first frame. Short and specific, on the same page.

bullets.title: Deliverables spelled out
bullets.body: Raw clips or the cut, how many variations, captions burned in or not. Written down so nothing is assumed.

features.visual: White card 400×300. Top: two small reference thumbnails as line-drawn phone frames with a play triangle in jam, labelled 'Ref 1' and 'Ref 2'. Below: two columns, 'DO' with three lines and small ticks, 'DON'T' with three lines and small crosses. Footer: 'Deliverables · raw + cut · captions on'.

features.title: Rights and authorisation, agreed before the shoot.
features.body: If the brief does not say whether the fee includes paid use or a Spark Ads code, that conversation happens after the footage lands, which is the most expensive time to have it. Usage, platforms and duration go in the brief and the creator's agreement at the same time.

bullets.title: Usage in the brief, not after
bullets.body: Organic only, whitelisting or a full buyout, the platforms covered and the number of days, on the brief itself.

bullets.title: Authorisation dated
bullets.body: Who generates the Spark Ads code or accepts the partnership invite, and by which date relative to the shoot.

bullets.title: The same terms the creator signed
bullets.body: The brief and the creator release carry identical usage lines, so there is one version of the truth.

features.visual: White card 400×290 titled 'USAGE'. Three rows with a label left and a value right: 'Scope · Organic + paid', 'Platforms · TikTok, Reels, Shorts', 'Duration · 90 days'. Below, a row of two chips: 'Spark Ads code · due before shoot', 'Release · signed'. A small jam dot before 'signed'.

features.title: Agreed with you, then sent to casting.
features.body: The brief is a working document until you sign it off, and a fixed one afterwards. Once agreed it goes to casting with the shortlist of hooks attached, and the tracker shows it move from brief to cast to shoot without you asking.

bullets.title: One round of changes, then locked
bullets.body: You read it, we change it, you sign it off. After that the script does not drift, which is why the first cut usually holds.

bullets.title: Sent to casting with the hooks
bullets.body: Casting starts from the brief, not from a follower count. The creator profile is written into it.

bullets.title: Visible on the tracker
bullets.body: Brief drafted, brief agreed, casting open. Every stage has a date on the live tracker you have access to.

features.visual: White card 400×280 showing a four-step progress row: 'Brief drafted' (tick), 'Brief agreed' (tick, jam), 'Casting open' (current, filled dot), 'Shoot' (empty). Under it a small activity list: '09:10 Brief v2 sent', '11:42 Agreed by your brand', '11:45 Sent to casting · 8 hooks attached'.

problems_head.h2: Built for the problems a brief actually has.
problems_head.p: Not a form. hypjam's briefs are built around the things that cost a shoot the most: the hook nobody wrote, the claim nobody checked, the tone nobody could describe, and the rights nobody mentioned until the invoice.

problems.icon: A speech bubble with an empty dotted line inside it
problems.title: The hook was described, not written
problems.body: 'Make it attention-grabbing' turns into eight different openings from eight creators. Ours arrives as a line, with alternatives, before the shoot.

problems.icon: A document with a warning triangle at its corner
problems.title: A claim that could not be made
problems.body: A results line that sounded fine on a call and cannot run as an ad. Must-say claims are listed and checked before they reach a script.

problems.icon: Three overlapping phone frames of different sizes
problems.title: Five creators, five tones
problems.body: Tone described in adjectives gets interpreted five ways. Two reference videos and a specific don't list keep the batch consistent.

problems.icon: A contract page with a clock in its corner
problems.title: Rights raised after the footage lands
problems.body: Whitelisting negotiated after the shoot costs more and delays the launch. Usage and authorisation dates are on the brief.

steps_head.h2: From a call to a locked script in one week.

steps.title: We talk
steps.body: A thirty-minute call about the product, the offer, the audience and the dates. No deck, no order form.

steps.title: We write
steps.body: The one thing, eight hooks, a five-beat shot list, must-say claims, references and the don'ts. Two pages.

steps.title: You mark it up
steps.body: One round of changes, then sign-off. The script is fixed from here so the shoot does not drift.

steps.title: It goes to casting
steps.body: The agreed brief and the hook shortlist go to casting the same day, and the tracker shows it move.

comparison_head.h2: Built for a phone shoot, not adapted to it.
comparison_head.p: Every part of the brief is tuned for how UGC is actually made: one person, one phone, a kitchen, and a first line that has to earn the next three seconds.

comparison.label: Length
comparison.body: Long enough for the hook, beats, claims, references and don'ts. Short enough that a creator reads all of it before filming.

comparison.label: Hooks
comparison.body: Written across different patterns, shortlisted with you, and shot as separate takes so a hook can be swapped in the edit.

comparison.label: Structure
comparison.body: Problem, discovery, demo, payoff, call to action. Intent per beat, phrasing left to the creator except where a claim is fixed.

comparison.label: Claims
comparison.body: Anything with legal or compliance weight is written word for word and checked against your landing page before sign-off.

comparison.label: Platforms
comparison.body: Ratio, length and pacing per placement: TikTok, Reels, Shorts, Snapchat, Pinterest and Meta ads each get their own note.

comparison.label: Rights
comparison.body: Scope, platforms and duration of use sit on the brief and the creator's signed release, with authorisation dates.

quote.text: We started hypjam because brands kept hiring creators one by one and nobody was directing the work. We treat UGC like a production: one brief, one team, a script before anyone films, an edit built for the feed.
quote.name: Avi Aggarwal

faq_head.h2: Questions brands ask before the first brief.

faq.q: Do I have to write anything myself?
faq.a: No. You tell us about the product, the offer and the audience on a call, and we write the brief. You read it, mark it up once and sign it off.

faq.q: How long does a brief take?
faq.a: A draft after the call, one round of changes, then sign-off, with the dates agreed on the call. It runs to two pages.

faq.q: Is the script written word for word?
faq.a: Only where it has to be. The hook and any must-say claims are exact. The rest is a five-beat shot list the creator phrases in their own words, which is what keeps it sounding like a person.

faq.q: Can we use our own brief?
faq.a: Yes. We will fold it into our template so the hook, beats, claims, references, don'ts, deliverables and usage terms are all in one place before the shoot.

faq.q: What if we change our mind after sign-off?
faq.a: Small changes before the shoot are fine. After the shoot a new hook or claim means new footage, and we will tell you plainly what it costs before doing it.

faq.q: Does the brief cover usage rights?
faq.a: Yes. Scope of use, the named platforms and the number of days sit on the brief and mirror the creator's signed release, so nothing is negotiated after the footage lands.

cta.p: Book a call and tell us what you are launching. We will come back with the one thing, the hooks and the shot list for it.

items.title: Hook writing for UGC ads | Eight opening lines per script | hypjam
items.description: Eight opening lines per UGC script across six hook patterns, shortlisted with you and shot as separate takes so a hook can be swapped without a reshoot.
items.h1: The first three seconds, written eight ways
items.intro: A hook is the line or moment that decides whether anyone sees the rest of the ad. It matters more than the product shot, the edit or the caption, because none of those get seen if it fails. hypjam writes eight hooks for every script, across different patterns, shortlists them with you and shoots them as separate takes so the opening can change without a reshoot.
items.hero_visual: A white card 420×420 titled 'HOOKS · your brand' with a small 'Script 01' tag. Eight numbered rows type in one after another (14px Geist); two rows (03 and 07) gain a jam tick and a 'picked' chip once typed. Beneath the card a small strip reads 'Shortlist agreed · shot as separate takes'. Same loop as the writers' room panel in the hero, larger.
items.statement: Eight opening lines for every script, and two that go to the shoot.

facts.label: Hooks written per script
Hook patterns we write across
Hooks in our published playbook
Picked with you before the shoot

features.title: Written as a line, not a vibe.
features.body: Creators improvise better from a strong first line than from 'be natural'. Every hook we hand over is an actual sentence a person can say, timed to land inside three seconds, with a note on what not to do in the first frame.

bullets.title: The exact opening line
bullets.body: No 'something attention-grabbing'. A sentence, written for speech, that a creator can deliver like a thought.

bullets.title: A first-frame note
bullets.body: No logo reveal, no 'hey guys', no slow zoom. Most weak hooks fail on pacing, not the idea, so the note is on the line.

bullets.title: One idea per hook
bullets.body: A curiosity hook does not also try to be a comparison. Each line does one job so the test tells you something.

features.visual: White card 400×280. A single hook line in 18px serif on a sand highlight, with a small '0–3s' timing tag. Under it three chips: 'Spoken, not read', 'No logo in frame 1', 'One idea'. Footer in grey: 'Hook 03 · problem-first'.

features.title: Six patterns, so the eight are not the same line.
features.body: Curiosity, problem-first, social proof, pattern interrupt, POV and comparison. Each script draws on several of them, because eight variations of one idea is one test, not eight.

bullets.title: Curiosity and problem-first
bullets.body: Open a loop the viewer wants closed, or name the frustration so they self-select before they know what you sell.

bullets.title: Social proof and pattern interrupt
bullets.body: Borrow trust from a wave of adoption, or break the feed's rhythm with a visual or a line that does not belong.

bullets.title: POV and comparison
bullets.body: Put the viewer in the moment, or stack the product against what they use now. Both are written to the platform they run on.

features.visual: White card 400×320 titled 'PATTERNS'. A 2×3 grid of small tiles: 'Curiosity', 'Problem-first', 'Social proof', 'Pattern interrupt', 'POV', 'Comparison', each with a one-line grey example beneath. Two tiles carry a small jam dot to show which the current script leans on.

features.title: Shortlisted with you before anyone films.
features.body: You see all eight with a one-line note on why each one exists and where it would run. You mark the ones you would actually put spend behind. The creator gets that shortlist, and the shoot is planned around it.

bullets.title: A note on every line
bullets.body: Which pattern it is, which placement it suits and which claim it leads to, so choosing is quick.

bullets.title: Two go to the shoot as standard
bullets.body: Two hooks per creator is the default; more can be added to a shoot day if the brief calls for it.

bullets.title: Compliance read before the list
bullets.body: A hook that implies a result we cannot support does not reach the shortlist.

features.visual: White card 400×330: eight rows with a checkbox left; rows 02 and 05 checked in jam with a 'shoot' chip; each row has a small grey pattern tag ('POV', 'Comparison', …) on the right. Footer: 'Approved by your brand · 11:42'.

features.title: Shot as separate takes.
features.body: The opening line is filmed on its own, then the body of the ad. That means one shoot produces several ads with different openings, and a hook that under-performs can be swapped in the edit rather than reshot.

bullets.title: Hook takes first
bullets.body: Each shortlisted hook is recorded as its own take, with two or three deliveries, before the beats.

bullets.title: Same body, different opening
bullets.body: The edit joins any hook to the same beats, so you get testable variations from one booking.

bullets.title: Logged by number
bullets.body: Every hook take is named on the tracker ('hook 03 · take 2') so the editor and you can find it.

features.visual: White card 400×300 shaped like a take list: 'Hook 03 · take 1', 'Hook 03 · take 2 ✓', 'Hook 07 · take 1 ✓', then a divider and 'Beats 01–05 · take 1 ✓'. Ticks in jam. A small phone frame top-right with a REC dot and a running timecode.

features.title: Written for the placement.
features.body: A pattern-interrupt hook suits the For You page. A POV hook fits the more composed feed on Reels. A Short needs to land faster than a Pinterest pin. Each hook carries the placement it was written for.

bullets.title: Platform on every line
bullets.body: TikTok, Reels, Shorts, Snapchat, Pinterest or Meta ads, named next to the hook rather than assumed.

bullets.title: Timing to the placement
bullets.body: The first line is timed to the platform's skip point, and the pacing note says how fast the first cut should come.

bullets.title: Captions considered from the start
bullets.body: A hook that reads well as an on-screen caption is written that way, because much of the feed is watched on mute.

features.visual: White card 400×300. Three rows, each a hook line with a platform chip on the right ('TikTok', 'Reels', 'Shorts') and a small timing bar under the line showing where the first cut lands. One chip is filled black to show the active placement.

features.title: Read, kept and fed into the next brief.
features.body: After a batch runs, the hooks that held attention and the ones that did not go into the debrief, by pattern. The next script starts from what worked, not from a blank page.

bullets.title: Hook rate, by hook
bullets.body: The three-second view rate is read per opening line, so a weak hook rate points at the line, not the product or the creator.

bullets.title: Patterns that repeat
bullets.body: If problem-first lines keep winning for your brand, the next eight lean that way. If comparison keeps losing, we stop writing it.

bullets.title: A library that is yours
bullets.body: Every hook we write for you stays in your brief history. Nothing is reused for another brand.

features.visual: White card 400×300 titled 'DEBRIEF · HOOKS'. A short table: hook number, pattern tag, and a small horizontal bar with no numbers on it (relative length only). Footer line: 'Carried into script 02: problem-first, POV'.

problems_head.h2: Built for the problems a hook actually has.
problems_head.p: Not a list of clickbait. hypjam's hooks are built around the ways an opening fails: it was never written, it tried to say everything, it was read aloud, or it was the same line eight times.

problems.icon: A phone frame with a diagonal skip arrow leaving it
problems.title: Scrolled past in the first second
problems.body: A logo, a slow zoom or 'hey guys' and the viewer is gone. Every hook has a first-frame note and is timed to the placement's skip point.

problems.icon: Eight identical short lines stacked
problems.title: Eight versions of the same idea
problems.body: Variations on one line are one test. Our eight draw on six patterns so the batch tells you which kind of opening works for you.

problems.icon: A speech bubble with a small script page inside it
problems.title: It sounds read aloud
problems.body: A hook written for the page dies in the mouth. Ours are written for speech and briefed with delivery notes, then recorded two or three ways.

problems.icon: A film strip with the first frame cut away by scissors
problems.title: A weak opening means a reshoot
problems.body: When the hook is baked into one long take, changing it means booking the creator again. Ours are separate takes, swapped in the edit.

faq.q: Why eight hooks and not one?
faq.a: One hook is one bet. Eight across several patterns lets the shoot carry two and the edit swap them, so the first batch tells you which kind of opening works for your brand.

faq.q: Do creators have to say the hook word for word?
faq.a: The idea and the timing are fixed; the delivery is theirs. We record two or three deliveries of each shortlisted hook and pick the one that sounds least like reading.

faq.q: Can we write our own hooks?
faq.a: Yes. Send them and we will fold them into the eight, give each a pattern and placement note, and shortlist them alongside ours.

faq.q: What happens if a hook does not work?
faq.a: Because hooks are shot as separate takes, a new opening is an edit, not a reshoot. The debrief says which patterns held and the next script starts from those.

faq.q: Do hooks change by platform?
faq.a: Yes. A line for the For You page is not the same as a line for Reels or a Short. Each hook names the placement it was written for and is timed to it.

faq.q: Are hooks checked for claims?
faq.a: Every shortlisted hook gets a compliance read against the must-say claims and UK ad disclosure rules before it goes to the shoot.

faq.q: Do we need usage rights as well?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Spark Ads and partnership ads let you run the creator's post from their handle. Usage rights let you use the file itself from your own handle, on your site or anywhere else. They are separate lines in the release and you can have one without the other.

faq.q: What happens when a window ends?

faq.q: Can a creator pull an ad mid-campaign?
faq.a: On TikTok the ad stops if the code is revoked; on Meta access can be pulled at any time. That is why the release includes a notice period before either happens.

faq.q: Is a whitelisted ad still labelled as an ad?
